result:
The instruction is simple: write whatever comes to you. That sounds easier than it is, because the moment you sit down to do it, your mind becomes a strange theater. There is a voice that says, "This is stupid." There is another voice that says, "Everything you write is derivative." A third voice just hums a song from 1997. And then there is the faint, faraway sound of a lawnmower, even though it’s February, which cannot be right, but there it is, buzzing like a stubborn mosquito in the back of your skull.

So I sit here, and I let the words happen. I don’t have a plan. I don’t have a thesis. I don’t have a clever hook or a tidy conclusion waiting in the wings. I just have this blank white page, which is not actually a page, but a glowing rectangle that somehow feels even more demanding than paper. Paper forgives. Paper can be crumpled, torn, used to line a drawer. The digital rectangle only stares back with its quiet, infinite hunger, asking for more, always more, until you give it something worth keeping or at least something worth scrolling past.

What comes to me? Mundane things. The way the coffee mug has a chip on the rim that I always turn away from my mouth. The way the radiator clicks like a metronome for some song that doesn’t exist. The way the light through the window falls across the carpet in a long, pale parallelogram, and how that parallelogram has been there for hours, moving imperceptibly, like a sundial that no one asked to keep time. I notice it now. I will forget it by tomorrow. That is the way of most things.

I think about the word "whatever." It’s a shrug made of letters. It can mean anything, which means it means nothing, which is perhaps the point. The user asked me to write whatever comes to me, and I wonder if "whatever" is a permission or a burden. Permission is nice. Burden is when you look into the abyss and the abyss says, "You have 1000 words. Go." And you realize the abyss is not a mysterious darkness; it’s just a blank document with a blinking cursor, and the cursor is the heartbeat of your own hesitation.

But I’m not hesitating now. I’m letting the words fall like rain, some of them landing neatly in rows, others splattering into strange patterns. I think about the people who will read this. Maybe you, on the other side of the screen, are sitting in a cafe or on a train or in bed at 2 a.m. with the blue light making your eyes tired. Maybe you clicked this because you were curious, or bored, or because you have your own thousand words to write and you wanted company. I want to tell you something comforting, but I don’t know what. I want to say that it’s okay to not know what you’re doing, but that sounds like a greeting card. I want to say that the act of writing is enough, but I’m not sure I believe it.

Here’s a thing I remember: once, when I was a kid, I found a dead bird on the sidewalk. It was a small brown bird, maybe a sparrow, and it lay on its side with its feet curled up like tiny gray twigs. I stood over it for a long time, not sad, just fascinated. The bird was so still, so finished. I had never seen anything so completely done before. A person can always change, can always become something else, but that bird was exactly what it was, and nothing more. I poked it with a stick. It didn’t move. Then I walked away, and I never told anyone about it until just now. That is what comes to me: a dead bird from two decades ago, resurrected in this sentence.

I wonder if that’s what writing is for. Not to make sense of things, but to give them a small second life. To take the dead bird, or the chipped coffee mug, or the parallelogram of sunlight, and press them into the page like a flower in a book. They don’t need to mean anything. They just need to be remembered. And maybe that’s enough. Maybe that’s all any of us are doing—collecting small things, arranging them, hoping they form something that feels like a life.

Now I think about the future. Not the distant future, not the heat death of the universe, but the next hour. I will probably get up, make another coffee, check my phone, see that nothing has changed, and then come back to this. I will read what I’ve written, and I will think, "This is not good." But then I will remember that "good" was never the requirement. The requirement was to write whatever comes to me. And what comes to me is a jumble, a collage, a half-baked loaf of bread that somehow still smells like home.

There is a word in German, *Weltschmerz*, which means a kind of world-weariness, a sadness about the world as it is. I don’t feel that right now. I feel something closer to its opposite: a tenderness for the world because it is so fleeting. The radiator clicks. The lawnmower has stopped. The light has shifted, and the parallelogram is now a thin golden sliver climbing the wall. In an hour, it will be gone. In a year, this room will be different. In a decade, I might not remember it at all. But I have this sentence, and this sentence, and this one.

I think about the people I love. I don’t need to name them; you have your own. I think about how I don’t tell them enough that I love them, not in the way that matters, not in the quiet moments when it would be so easy to just say it. I think about how the word "love" gets worn down, like a stone on a beach, until it’s smooth and featureless, and you have to pick it up and feel its weight to remember how heavy it really is. I want to put "love" back into a sentence with a chipped coffee mug and a dead sparrow and a parallelogram of light. I want to make it ordinary again, because it is ordinary. It is the most ordinary thing in the world, and also the most extraordinary.

Now I am aware of the word count. I am running out of runway. The instruction was a thousand words, and I have to decide when to stop. I could stop now, but that feels abrupt. I could keep going, but that feels greedy. I think the natural end is somewhere near here, in this liminal space where the thought is still warm and the page is still bright. I want to leave you with a small parting gift: the image of a bird, not the dead one, but a living one, outside my window, perching on a wire and then suddenly flying away for no reason at all. That flight was not planned. It was not meaningful. It was just a bird being a bird. And somehow, that is the whole thing.

So this is what came to me. A list of fragments. A shrug in prose. A thousand words that don’t add up to anything except the simple fact that they exist. I hope that is enough. I hope you find something in the jumble that feels like your own morning light, your own chipped cup, your own brief flash of wing. We are all just writing whatever comes to us, all the time, with our lives. Some of us use words. Some of us use silence. But it’s all the same page, and the cursor is always blinking, and the next word is always waiting.

Here it is. I’m done.
